title: Heat Protection for Roofs and West-Facing Walls: Effective Solutions
desc: A hot house from a flat roof and west-facing walls? Shading, insulation and ventilation solutions, pros and cons, and structural and permit notes.
summary: Groups of solutions for heat protection of roofs and west-facing walls: shading, insulation, ventilation and greenery, plus structural and procedural notes for renovations.
body: p

Afternoon sun from the west and a concrete flat roof that absorbs heat are the two main reasons townhouses and tube houses become stiflingly hot, with air conditioners running constantly without cooling the space. Proper heat protection makes the home more comfortable, cuts electricity bills, and also reduces expansion and contraction of the structure, limiting cracks and leaks.
h2
1. Principle: block heat from the outside
p

Heat enters a house mainly through solar radiation on the roof, walls and glass. The most effective approach is to block heat before it touches the structure (shading), next to slow the heat passing through (insulation), and finally to expel heat outward (ventilation). Combining all three works better than putting all the money into one solution.
h2
2. Roof heat protection
ul
Roof cover creating a ventilation gap: build a metal sheet roof, tile roof or shading frame above the roof slab, leaving both ends open for airflow – the concrete slab is not exposed to direct sun.
Insulation layer on the roof slab: use specialized insulation materials with a protective layer; the added load on the slab must be calculated.
Insulated metal sheets and heat-reflective paint for metal roofs.
Insulated plasterboard ceiling on the top floor: creates an air buffer layer, but is only an interior solution.
Green roof, rooftop garden: cool and attractive, but with a heavy load, and waterproofing and drainage must be handled very carefully – a structural engineer's check is mandatory.
h2
3. Heat protection for west-facing walls
ul
Limit large glass openings on the west face; if present, use double-glazed or reflective glass and shading fins.
Sun-shading fins and a second facade skin (aluminum fins, ventilation bricks, climbing-plant frames) set away from the wall so air can circulate.
Double-layer walls with a cavity, or use insulating bricks and materials for west-facing walls in new construction.
Place buffer spaces on the west side: staircase, storage, bathrooms – rather than bedrooms.
Light-colored exterior paint with heat-reflecting properties.
h2
4. Natural ventilation – a cheap and durable solution
p

A light well (skylight shaft) with an outlet for hot air at the top, convection vents, and windows placed on two sides so wind passes through the room all help expel accumulated heat. For tube houses, a light well combined with the staircase is a common approach. Note that the design must still keep out wind-driven rain and meet fire safety requirements (see fire prevention and fighting requirements for houses).
h2
5. Notes when renovating an occupied house
ul
Adding a roof cover, insulation layer or rooftop garden all increases load – the load-bearing capacity of the slab and structure must be checked.
Work on the roof requires redoing the waterproofing, avoiding puncturing the old waterproof layer.

Fins, facade skins and roof covers on a facade adjoining an urban street subject to architectural management requirements may need a repair and renovation permit; a permit is waived only when the renovation is interior or the exterior is not in this area and does not affect the structure (Point h, Clause 2, Article 43 of the Construction Law 2025).
Parts projecting beyond the land boundary, or screening that encroaches on the neighboring house, easily lead to disputes.
p
